questions.question: Why does full attention become such a severe bottleneck at 64k context and beyond?
options: Its compute scales quadratically with sequence length
It cannot be combined with causal masking
It forces the model to use learned position embeddings
It disables grouped-query attention
questions.explanation: The lesson states that attention can consume 70-80% of decode latency at 64k because each query compares against an enormous number of keys. That O(N^2) pattern eventually dominates both compute and memory bandwidth.

questions.question: Why do inference-time sparse tricks on a dense-pretrained model usually leave performance on the table?
options: Because sparse kernels cannot run on GPUs
Because the model was never trained to route information through the sparse pattern
Because dense models cannot use sliding windows
Because top-k selection is always nondifferentiable
questions.explanation: If a model learned with dense attention, turning on sparsity only at inference asks it to use a routing pattern it never practiced. NSA is meant to be trained natively so the model learns how to use the sparse structure from the start.

questions.question: Which three branches make up Native Sparse Attention?
options: Dense attention, cross-attention, and recurrence
Compressed branch, selected fine-grained branch, and sliding-window branch
MoE routing, quantization, and KV eviction
RoPE branch, RMSNorm branch, and SwiGLU branch
questions.explanation: NSA combines a coarse global view, a routed fine-grained read of the most relevant blocks, and a local window for nearby structure. A learned gate mixes those three outputs rather than forcing one branch to handle everything.

questions.question: Why does the lesson call NSA "natively trainable" even though it uses a top-k block selection?
options: Because gradients flow through the compressed-branch attention scores that drive both routing and output quality
Because top-k is replaced by beam search during backward
Because only the sliding-window branch is trained
Because the model stores every token densely anyway
questions.explanation: The key is that the compressed branch is fully differentiable and its scores determine which blocks get selected. The discrete top-k controls memory reads, but the learning signal still flows through the coarse attention map that produced those scores.

questions.question: Using the lesson's 64k example with l=64, k=16, b=64, and w=512, about how many keys does NSA attend to per query?
options: About 2,536 keys, roughly a 25x reduction from full attention
About 6,400 keys, roughly a 10x reduction
About 64,000 keys, so there is no reduction
About 512 keys, exactly the sliding-window size only
questions.explanation: The compressed branch contributes N/l = 1000 keys, the selected branch contributes k*b = 1024, and the sliding window contributes 512. Summed together that is 2,536 keys per query, far below the 64,000 keys of full attention.
